newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Temporary deal reached to save Venezuelan airline.
newsitem.headline: Temporary deal reached to save Venezuelan airline.

text.p: A preliminary agreement to save troubled Venezuelan airline Viasa from bankruptcy was reached on Tuesday but the company kept all its planes grounded.

Venezuela's National Investment Fund (FIV), the body in charge of privatizations, said the deal was worked out in Madrid during talks between FIV President Alberto Poletto and representatives of Spain's national carrier Iberia.
Iberia, which took over Viasa management in 1991, holds the largest stake in the loss-making airline with 45 percent.
Viasa suspended all its flights on Jan. 23, stranding hundreds of passengers. Its long-standing woes worsened earlier this month when workers overwhelmingly rejected an emergency cost-cutting plan.
The FIV said in a statement the "proposed measures are essential to avoid Viasa's bankruptcy and guarantee its survival."

They included an FIV pledge to set up a trust fund and an Iberia agreement to "recapitalize part of Viasa's debt" in exchange for the fleet of aircraft that was being held as a guarantee. No specific figures were provided.

The two sides also agreed to look "as early as possible" for an operating partner for Viasa and decided to maintain all Viasa flights suspended "until the plan is approved ... and a definite solution can be found" to guarantee the future of the airline.
But the two sides also acknowledged the plan hinged on agreement from Viasa's workers.
Company officials earlier said shareholders were expected to vote on Friday on whether to declare the carrier bankrupt.
The airline's decision to suspend flights left about 600 travelers stranded, mostly Argentine tourists, Viasa said.
"I've spent four extra days in Venezuela, how am I going to justify that to my boss?" asked one stranded passenger, worried that she might lose her job.

Other travelers were transferred free of charge to five-star hotels. "It's a delight ... we want to stay another week," Argentine tourist Belia Baudracco said on Margarita island, Venezuela's prime Caribbean tourist destination.
Venezuela, through the FIV, has a 40 percent share in Viasa and the country's largest bank, Banco Provincial, owns 15 percent.
Viasa, which employs about 2,200 people and was founded 35 years ago, registered a $30 million loss last year and has not reported a profit since Iberia took over. Its debts total about $150 million.
